title: Are Europe’s extreme summers the new normal? What the science says
facts: Temperatures reached 40 degrees Celsius across Germany, the Czech Republic, and Poland on the final Sunday of June 2026.
One town in France recorded a peak temperature of 44 degrees Celsius during the early-summer heatwave of 2026.
The early-summer heatwave in France left an estimated 1,000 excess deaths.
The 2025 summer heatwave caused an estimated 2,300 climate-related deaths across 12 European countries according to World Weather Attribution.
World Weather Attribution found that intense heat on the level of the 2026 summer is tens to hundreds of times more likely than it was in 2003.
Heat-related deaths in Europe have risen by an average of 52 per million people annually since the 1990s.
Dr Hans Kluge serves as the World Health Organization’s regional director for Europe.
Heatwaves in Europe were generally about 3.5 degrees Celsius cooler in June 1976 compared to current extremes.
Europe has warmed at approximately twice the global average since the 1980s according to Copernicus.
At current emissions rates, heatwaves of the 2026 magnitude are expected to occur every couple of decades.
Stalled high-pressure systems known as heat domes are the immediate trigger for trapping heat in concentrated areas.
The Copernicus European State of the Climate 2025 report confirmed that more than 95 percent of Europe saw above-average annual temperatures last year.
Europe experienced its highest recorded sea-surface temperatures in 2025.
The Lancet Countdown Europe calculated that 62,000 heat-related deaths occurred across the region in 2024.
Dr Hans Kluge advised European governments to plan for heatwaves with permanent infrastructure rather than treating them as one-off emergencies.
